idiom_name: Warden/Devise current_user (session holds the id) + ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes as carrier
implementation_notes: Rails' descriptor is the object Warden returns for the configured scope: Devise defines current_user / user_signed_in? helpers on top of request.env['warden'], and the session stores only the record id, so the user is reloaded per request. Where non-controller code (models, service objects, jobs) needs the actor, ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes gives a thread-isolated per-request singleton (Current.user) that resets around each request. The classic authenticator/descriptor/factory structure is replaced by the Rack middleware plus these helpers; hand-roll a plain value object when the descriptor must be smaller than the ActiveRecord model.
code_sketch:
class Current < ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes
  attribute :user
end

class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action { Current.user = current_user }        # Devise + Warden
end

# anywhere inside the request (model, service object):
Current.user&.id || "anonymous"
pitfalls: current_user is unavailable outside the Rack request cycle (background jobs, ActionCable channels, rake tasks) - CurrentAttributes does not cross those boundaries automatically and must be set explicitly.

CurrentAttributes is isolated per thread or fiber; with async servers a value set for one request can leak or go missing if the reset hooks are skipped, and it is no substitute for passing the actor into jobs.
Devise memoizes current_user for the request, and in multi-scope apps current_user versus current_admin are different descriptors - name the actor explicitly so a check cannot test the wrong one.
